   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?

   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?

   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?

   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?

   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Amphenol shows some Rule Breaker traits: it is a top beneficiary of AI data-center build-outs, has strong price momentum (about +25% over a year) and excellent long-term execution. It is weaker on others: it is not the clear leader of an emerging industry (TE Connectivity is larger), the brand is unknown to consumers and it has no distinctive mission.
summaries.buffett: Amphenol fits much of Buffett's approach: an understandable, consistently profitable business with a long record, rational acquisitions and a long-serving CEO. The weak points are price and balance sheet: the stock trades near 40 times trailing earnings and debt of $18.8B exceeds cash of $5.4B after the CommScope CCS purchase.
summaries.munger: Munger would like the high-quality, decentralised operating culture and the long record of compounding returns on capital. He would weigh that against a full valuation and the cyclicality and customer concentration risk of AI data-center demand.
summaries.lynch: Amphenol now looks like a fast grower riding AI interconnect, with revenue expected to rise about 54% in 2026 (partly from acquisitions). Its P/E of about 30 times 2026 estimates is close to, but not clearly below, its earnings growth rate, and it is no longer an overlooked niche stock.
summaries.fisher: Amphenol scores well on Fisher's points: decades of growth, continual new products, strong margins (25.4% operating in 2025) and a deep, long-tenured management team. It is less distinctive on visible R&D leadership and on candour beyond solid quarterly reporting.
summaries.graham: Amphenol fails Graham's defensive-investor tests on price: about 40 times trailing earnings and roughly 12.6 times book value. It passes on size, profitability every year and an unbroken dividend since 2005, but valuation rules it out.
summaries.thiel: Amphenol is a strong operator in a competitive market rather than a monopoly with 10x better technology. Its edge is speed, breadth and execution in custom connectors, and its timing in AI interconnect is very good.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner would note Amphenol is a direct beneficiary of the AI compute build-out, with accelerating revenue and rising estimates. He would watch the valuation, the leverage from the CommScope deal and the risk of an AI capex digestion phase.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings are accelerating sharply (Q2 2026 sales +55%, orders $10.7B) and analysts' estimates have risen over the last 90 days, which fits Druckenmiller's focus on earnings momentum. The stock fell from its summer peak, and the key question is how long AI capex keeps growing.
summaries.smith: Amphenol meets Smith's 'good company' test with high returns on capital, rising margins and strong cash conversion. It is less clear on 'don't overpay' given a free-cash-flow yield of only about 2%.
summaries.greenblatt: Amphenol has a high return on capital (about 33% pre-tax operating income on invested capital in 2025, calculated) but a low earnings yield: 2025 operating income is under 3% of enterprise value. It would not rank highly on the Magic Formula.
summaries.akre: On Akre's three-legged stool, the business is high quality with a long compounding record, management is talented and owner-like, and there is a long reinvestment runway through acquisitions and organic growth. The main concern is the current high valuation.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for heads-I-win, tails-I-don't-lose-much bets at deep discounts, and Amphenol at about 40 times trailing earnings is not distressed or cheap. It is a quality business but not a Dhandho-style bargain.
summaries.wood: Amphenol is an enabler of AI, but as a connector maker it is not itself a disruptive innovation platform of the kind ARK targets. Its costs do not fall exponentially with volume.
summaries.ackman: Amphenol fits several of Ackman's criteria: a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating business with high barriers to switching and strong management. It is less of a fit on balance-sheet conservatism after the CommScope debt and on buying at a discount.
summaries.sleep: Amphenol grows by scale and decentralised execution but does not run a Costco-style scale-economics-shared model that passes savings to customers. Sleep would value its long-term orientation but find the model less distinctive.
summaries.valentine: Amphenol sells into a large, painful problem: moving ever more data and power through AI, auto and defense systems. As a mature public company it is far from Valentine's early-stage venture lens.
summaries.nash: Amphenol scores well on growth, margins and trend (AI infrastructure layer) and an estimated 90 points on Nash's 13 categories. It fails his instant-kill rule of more debt than cash after the CommScope CCS acquisition, and a simple DCF gives a value below today's price.

momentum.evidence: The stock is up about 25% over the last year (Yahoo Finance, Oct 16, 2026 close $79.35), but it has fallen from a split-adjusted peak of about $88 in June 2026.

g4.evidence: It is run by a respected long-serving team (CEO Adam Norwitt since 2009, CFO Craig Lampo since 2015) and widely held by institutions, but has no famous anchor investor.

g6.evidence: With a trailing P/E of about 40, some commentators call it expensive, but the average analyst price target of $102.97 is above the price.

simple.evidence: It makes connectors, cables, antennas and sensors sold to equipment makers, a business a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Sales grew from $8,598.9M in 2020 to $23,094.7M in 2025 with profits every year and operating margins between 19% and 25%.

integrity.evidence: Management reports clearly, returns cash (nearly $1.5B in 2025 via $665.2M buybacks and $802.2M dividends) and has a disciplined acquisition record, but the CEO is also chairman.

b6.evidence: Acquisitions are central to its strategy, including the ~$10.5B CommScope CCS deal, but they have historically been disciplined and accretive rather than empire-building.

roic.evidence: 2025 operating income of $5,868.6M was about 33% of invested capital (equity $13,500.4M plus debt $15,502.0M minus cash $11,434.2M, calculated), with modest leverage before the 2026 deal.

fcf.evidence: 2025 free cash flow was $4,392.9M, about 103% of net income of $4,270.3M.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings reinvested in capex and acquisitions helped lift revenue from $8,598.9M to $23,094.7M and operating income from $1,638.4M to $5,868.6M between 2020 and 2025.

safety.evidence: A simple DCF using 3-year averages (about 24% growth, 17% FCF margin) and a 12% discount rate gives about $43-51 per share versus a price of $79.35.

fairprice.evidence: At about 30 times 2026 and 24 times 2027 consensus EPS ($2.69 and $3.33), the price is high but partly justified by 24% expected EPS growth in 2027.

mu5.evidence: Diversification across seven end markets and no customer at 10% or more of sales limit the ways it could fail, but a sharp AI capex downturn plus higher debt could hurt results badly.

reinvest.evidence: It keeps reinvesting at high returns through capex ($996.6M in 2025) and acquisitions, with operating margins rising to 29.5% in Q2 2026.

ly2.evidence: It fits the fast-grower category with a simple story: more AI data centers, electrified cars and defense spending need more high-speed connectors.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 40 and forward P/E of about 30 (2026) are above the 24% EPS growth analysts expect for 2027.

runway.evidence: Consensus sees revenue rising from $23.1B in 2025 to $48.4B in 2028, and acquisitions keep adding new products and regions.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares rose from 2,460.0M in 2020 to 2,555.0M in 2025 (split-adjusted), and insiders are not known for open-market buying.

ly8.evidence: Connectors are a 'boring' niche, but Amphenol is now a ~$196B AI favourite covered by about 18 analysts.

fi2.evidence: It keeps launching new high-speed copper and fiber interconnect generations for AI and added fiber connectivity through CommScope CCS.

fi3.evidence: About 6,400 engineering staff support design wins that pushed Communications Solutions sales to $5,383.6M in Q2 2026 from $2,909.8M a year earlier.

fi4.evidence: Its decentralised units sit close to customers and win designs quickly, giving Q2 2026 orders of $10.7B and a 1.23:1 book-to-bill.

longterm.evidence: Management invests through cycles and acquires for the long term, but the culture is also known for tight quarterly cost discipline.

gr1.evidence: 2025 revenue was $23,094.7M and the market value is about $196B.

ni10.evidence: Amphenol has been profitable every year for well over a decade, including net income of $1,203.4M in 2020 and $4,270.3M in 2025.

gr4.evidence: Amphenol started a quarterly dividend of $.03 per share in 2005 (per its 2005 10-K) and has paid one every year since, 21 years through 2025 ($802.2M paid in 2025).

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $1.96 in 2020 (pre-2024-split basis, i.e. $0.98 on the 2024 basis) to $3.34 in 2025, far more than one third even over five years.

gr6.evidence: The trailing P/E is about 40, far above 15.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 40 times price/book of about 12.6 (market value ~$195.7B over equity $15,491.6M) is far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its products are competitive and fast to market but not ten times better than TE, Molex or Foxconn Interconnect.

timing.evidence: AI data-center build-outs need ever-faster interconnect, driving 55% sales growth in Q2 2026 and guidance of 50-52% growth for Q3 2026.

th3.evidence: It started as a niche military connector maker and expanded across seven markets, but it never dominated a small market in the Thiel sense.

team.evidence: Norwitt has led since 2009 and grown sales to $23,094.7M, with a long-tenured, well-regarded management bench.

th5.evidence: Its local engineering and sales teams sit inside customers' design processes worldwide, which is a strong distribution advantage.

durable.evidence: Connectors will be needed for decades and Amphenol has adapted for 90+ years, but shifts like co-packaged optics could change which interconnects win.

th7.evidence: It moved early and heavily into AI rack interconnect and fiber (CommScope CCS), but rivals have seen the same opportunity.

trend.evidence: IT datacom, largely AI, was 36% of 2025 sales and is the main driver of growth.

dr1.evidence: Consensus 2026 EPS rose from $2.44 to $2.69 and 2027 from $2.92 to $3.33 over 90 days, and Q2 2026 GAAP EPS grew 59%.

dr2.evidence: CommScope CCS synergies (2026 sales now seen at $4.6B and $0.30 EPS accretion) and AI ramps should help, but much of this is already in estimates.

dr4.evidence: AI capex is strong, but higher rates raise the cost of its $18.8B debt and tariffs remain a cost risk.

dr6.evidence: Upcoming events include Q3 2026 results with guidance for $9.3B-$9.4B sales, next-generation AI platform ramps and CCS integration.

dr7.evidence: It is a high-quality compounder, but valuation and dependence on AI capex argue against a very large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin of 36.88% in 2025 is good for hardware and rising, but not software-like.

fcfyield.evidence: 2025 free cash flow of $4,392.9M is about 2.2% of the ~$195.7B market value.

gb2.evidence: 2025 operating income of $5,868.6M is about 2.8% of enterprise value of about $209B.

pa2.evidence: There is no setback to buy into; the business is growing rapidly.

pa4.evidence: The business is diversified and highly profitable, but at about 40 times earnings a fall in AI demand could cause a large, lasting price decline.

wo1.evidence: It is a leading supplier of AI data-center interconnect, but it enables AI rather than leading in AI itself.

wo2.evidence: Connector costs do not fall on a Wright's-law curve that opens up big new demand.

wo3.evidence: It is a components company, not a combination of several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its market can grow strongly but not many times over in five years; consensus sees revenue roughly doubling from 2025 to 2028.

ac3.evidence: It is exposed to metal costs, tariffs and interest rates on its debt, though it has passed through costs and recovered tariffs.

ns1.evidence: Rising margins (operating margin up from 19.05% in 2020 to 25.41% in 2025) show it keeps scale benefits rather than passing them to customers.

ns4.evidence: Scale from CommScope CCS and AI design wins should strengthen it, but competition from Chinese suppliers and design shifts make this uncertain.

va2.evidence: Moving vast data and power reliably inside AI clusters, vehicles and defense systems is a large, costly problem its products solve.

tn1.evidence: It sells into AI infrastructure (36% of 2025 sales from IT datacom), but it is a 90-year-old connector company adapting to the trend rather than built for it.

tn2.evidence: The market increasingly sees it as an AI infrastructure company, but it is still mainly a diversified connector maker, so the gap is small.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap US industrial technology company, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: It passes two of three: revenue grew to $23,094.7M in 2025 and it is profitable, but debt of $18,811.3M exceeds cash of $5,419.1M because of the CommScope acquisition.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive each quarter, but debt exceeded cash at December 31, 2025 ($15,502.0M versus $11,434.2M) and June 30, 2026 ($18,811.3M versus $5,419.1M).

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 51.7% in 2025 and 55% (30% organic) in Q2 2026.

tn7.evidence: 2025 revenue growth of 51.7% plus free-cash-flow margin of 19.0% is about 71.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue grew 51.7% while total costs (cost of sales plus operating expenses) grew about 42.8%, from $12,065.8M to $17,226.1M (calculated).

tn9.evidence: It fails the instant kill of more debt than cash ($18,811.3M debt versus $5,419.1M cash at June 30, 2026), though it passes the others.

tn10.evidence: No major legal threat, but US-China trade policy and tariffs matter as about 16% of 2025 sales were in China.

tn11.evidence: Amphenol provides custom connectors, cables and sensors that help equipment makers move data and power reliably, and charges per part sold; customers choose it for speed of design and breadth.

tn13.evidence: Estimated total 90: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 10, operating margin 10, short interest 10 (~1%), institutional ownership 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 10, moat 5, CEO 10, pricing power 5, secular trend 10, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue dipped in 2023 ($12,554.7M versus $12,623.0M) and debt exceeded cash in 2025.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage (H1 2026 operating income $4,416.4M over interest $421.6M) is about 10x, current ratio about 1.9 and liabilities 1.9x equity, but assets excluding goodwill ($27,251.9M) are below total liabilities ($29,184.5M).

tn18.evidence: Norwitt has 17 years as CEO and a strong record of growth and margins, but he is not a founder and is not known for open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Amphenol beat consensus EPS in each of the last four quarters, by 3% to 16% (Yahoo Finance).

tn21.evidence: No accounting or governance red flags are known and margins are rising, but it is a frequent acquirer (CommScope CCS, El.Com, Wilder in 2026).

tn22.evidence: It has $23.1B of revenue, strong profits and buys back shares rather than selling them.

tn24.evidence: The price implies roughly 23% (10% discount rate) to 32% (12%) annual growth for five years at a 19% FCF margin, below current reported growth but helped by acquisitions; organic growth was 30% in Q2 2026.

tn25.evidence: Nash's DCF with about 24% trimmed to 20% growth, 16.8% average FCF margin, 4% terminal growth and net debt gives about $43 per share at 12%, below $79.35.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 29.5 (2026 EPS $2.69) divided by 2027 EPS growth of about 24% gives a PEG of about 1.2, above 1.
